speechtext:
Canada must do more for peace than just rhetoric, the kind of rhetoric we have just heard. Canada must be seen as willing to do more, and I agree with the Minister that Canada has the capacity to do more. I continue to call upon him and the Government to use that capacity.
I call upon them to sign the protocol to the Contadora Treaty; to offer technical, financial and diplomatic help to the Central American Republics in meeting the requirements of the Arias Peace Plan in respect of amnesties, refugees, civil rights and press freedom, the conduct of elections, negotiations, arms control, and reduction verification; to urge the United States and Nicaragua to resume their essential bilateral talks, including offering Canada as a site for such talks; and to offer to increase direct economic assistance to the region, especially to Nicaragua, because of the vast foreign interference in that country, the U.S. economic blockade, the destabilizing and bankrupting of the economy, recognizing that a collapsing Nicaraguan economy and heightened security concerns will impede any peace settlement.
In conclusion, Canadians expect-and Central America desperately needs it-some greater Canadian diplomatic and political initiative. One initiative mentioned by the Hon. Member for Spadina was that we should take a leading role in rallying international support through the United Nations and in organizing a multilateral support group and peace fund in support of the peace accord verification process. On September 1 in the House my colleague said that such steps would help to sustain the Central American peace accord against attacks from the Reagan administration.
We want to help build and secure peace in our hemisphere. As I mentioned, Canadians do a great deal as individuals. Just the other day in Vancouver I visited a group of fishermen, longshoremen, carpenters, and other workers who in their spare time-perhaps it is a couple of hours a day; in some cases it is only a couple of hours a week-are building a great fishing boat for a village in Nicaragua. The villagers are expecting it. They do not have any boats now except ones which have long since ceased to be useful or practical. They still need money for the engine, and we are hoping to be able to raise it. However, we have that strong feeling of Canadians wanting to give help.
The Government can respond more. Signing the protocol to the Contadora Treaty would be an illuminating expression of
September 10, 1987

the Government's concern for the building and securing of peace in our hemisphere.
Finally, Canada's resources and strong traditions enable and indeed require us to play such a role.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF SIGNING PROTOCOL TO CONTADORA TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to bring the House up to date on progress accomplished in the peace process in Central America. I am all the more pleased that "progress" is the right word, if recent events are taken into account. As Hon. Members would know, the presidents of the five Central American countries recently agreed on a new peace plan for the region, supported by the other major interested countries, particularly the United States, Cuba and the Soviet Union. This is an extremely positive development.
Still I would not want to create the impression that this plan will solve all the problems of the region. In recent years the negotiations sponsored by the countries of the Contadora Group-Mexico, Panama, Columbia and Venezuela-raised expectations which too often turned into disillusions. Of course this does not take anything away from the efforts of the countries of the Contadora Group which, despite huge obstacles, displayed resolution and determination.
It seems to us that the worst of these obstacles is the existence of serious socio-economic disparities. Guerillas in Salvador, Nicaragua and Guatemala also stand in the way of a peaceful settlement. Finally, and this may be the key factor, the influence fight between the two superpowers tends to make regional conflicts even worse. Canada sincerely hopes that the good will shown by all parties in recent weeks will lead to an honest effort to overcome the obstacles.
Canada has a clear policy as concerns the situation in Central America. In his speech last year before the InterAmerican Press Association, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) described the Contadora initiative as the best tool for reconciliation in Central America. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has also expressed in public statements both in Canada and abroad the firm support of Canada for the Contadora process. Mr. Clark re-affirmed his position during his visits to Argentina, Uruguay and Venezuela in 1986. In January 1987, in a message addressed to the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the Contadora Group and the Lima Support Group, as well as the Secretaries General of the United Nations and the Organization of American States on the occasion of their mission to the countries of Central America, Mr. Clark stated that the efforts of the Contadora Group have sustained the hope of the international community to see a lasting solution to the crisis in Central America. Moreover, in 1986, the Canadian delegation to the General Asembly of the United Nations made a statement in support of the Contadora Group.
Contadora Treaty
Canada has also provided constructive and practical support to the Contadora Group and the peace process in general. During his visit to Mexico in 1985, Mr. Clark had an opportunity to discuss the situation in Central America and the Contadora Group plan with President de la Madrid and his Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Sepulveda. He emphasized the firm support of Canada to the Contadora initiative and its desire to play in due time a constructive role in the peace process. Mr. Clark stated that Canada is willing to share its peace-keeping operations experience with the parties involved. Since then, the Canadian Government has written at the request of the Contadora Group countries a series of comments on the provisions of the draft act on security and follow-up.
These comments are based on a number of considerations, such as the need to impart to our observations a neutral, objective and impartial character.
We also were aware of the need to ensure the viability of any verification and follow-up commission that could be established under the Contadora Act. More specifically, we thought that the funding for such an operation should be closely examined by all the parties involved for the selected mechanisms to be as efficient as possible in the circumstances.
We believe that the concept of a regional solution to that problem needs to be emphasized. In that respect, we feel that the Central American parties themselves should be involved as much as possible in the peacekeeping mechanisms, inasmuch as such involvement contributes to the efficient operation of a verification and follow-up commission. The commission should have specific and firm guarantees as to its freedom to travel within the area, and should also enjoy unimpaired communications with the media. Finally, we believe that a political authority should of necessity be appointed to sponsor the commission, whose mandate would be for a specific period.
The Government feels that the principles stated two years ago for the follow-up and verification are still relevant and should be applied to the present peace plan.
On August 7, at the end of the historic Guatemala Summit, the Central American nations' Presidents announced the conclusion of an agreement on a new peace plan for the area. The plan provides that the Ministers of Foreign Affairs will meet within fifteen days after the agreement is signed, to initiate the implementation of provisions dealing with an amnesty for the insurgents, a cease-fire, a dialogue with the unarmed opposition groups, which should come to an end after ninety days, that is November 7. The Contadora Group countries among others will be called upon to set up a verification and follow-up commission that will be responsible for monitoring the level of forces in place.
Mr. Speaker, the same day it was signed, we welcomed that Agreement which was supported by Mr. Clark. Later on, two envoys sent by Mr. Clark went to the area to express Canada's support and to offer technical advice on the development of the peace-keeping mechanisms. Countries in the area welcomed the envoys and Canada's offer.

September 10, 1987
Contadora Treaty
Other facts provide hope. As I said, under the Agreement, the Ministers of Foreign Affairs were to meet within fifteen days. That meeting took place on August 19 and 20, in San Salvador. Later, on August 22 and 23, in Caracas, the Ministers met their counterparts from the Contadora Group and the Lima Support Group, as well as representatives from the United Nations and the OAS, and agreed to set up a verification commission. Not being part of the area, Canada is not a member of the commission. However, we informed all the governments involved that we were willing if need be to provide the commission with technical advice.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we may safely conclude that real progress has been made. However, we should avoid deceiving ourselves. Guerilla warfare continues, as well as competition between the superpowers. The problem of poverty remains and is compounded by the massive influx of refugees fleeing the conflicts. Human rights, civil liberties and democratic institutions are still trampled in certain parts of the area. The latest events are a positive, albeit hesitating step in the right direction. The Canadian Government will continue to encourage and support Central America and Contadora Group countries and extend any technical advice they will deem useful.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF SIGNING PROTOCOL TO CONTADORA TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with great interest to the comments of both of my colleagues. I must say that I and others in this House undoubtedly have been heartened and encouraged by the positive developments that one sees emerging from the Guatemala peace plan of August 7. However, I must say that I am not quite as sanguine as the spokesman for the Government with respect to the evolution of the plan as it is designed. I say that largely because of my concerns with the continuing policy of our good neighbour to the south, the United States. Only today Mr. Shultz has testified that the Government wishes to increase its funding to the Contras by $270 million over the forthcoming 18 month period, which is an escalation over the amount of $100 million, the timetable for which expires on September 30. In fact, as I read the press report as it came over the wire, it appeared that Mr. Shultz justifies this because of the timetable. The cease-fire does not take effect until November 7. Hence it is the argument of the U.S. administration that this would leave the Nicaraguan Sandinis-ta regime unconstrained by the threat of the rebel Contra forces during that period, playing into the hands of the Communists. I can only say that this is hardly the basis upon which we should be building a secure and lasting peace in Central America.
I will go back and talk a bit about the history of some of the issues in a moment, but I would like to emphasize to the Conservative Government, and I am sure my colleague, the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), will agree with me, that one thing Canada can do
concretely is to exercise our supposed good offices in Washington to bring a stop to this increased funding to the extent possible. In that regard I am confident that the efforts of the Government will be supported by many if not an overwhelming majority of Americans as well as Congressmen.
I need not remind this House of the tremendous opposition which was expressed not only here but in the United States to the funding of the Contras in the first instance. Here, on the very eve of a major breakthrough, we are faced with a reaffirmation and an escalation of that policy which all of us in this House on both sides condemned in the first instance.
I commend the Government on any steps it may take to make Canadian expertise available for the purposes of verification. We know that Canada enjoys an international reputation in that regard, well earned in many corners of the Globe over many many, years, and I am happy that we have officials in Central America at the present time, but there is one major obstacle going far beyond the issue of verification, and that is, the current policy of the U.S. administration. It is with respect to that policy that Canada is in a unique position to exercise influence.
I can say to this House in a personal vein that I am gratified and have been gratified by the tremendous concern shown by my constituents and by Canadians across this land for the circumstances in Central America. I know that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) feels the same way. He has many constituents who continue to make representations to him saying Canada has a major role to play.
Apart from the human tragedy to which we must respond, the refugee issues, the suffering, the fact that a surrogate war is being conducted by untrained teenagers, the great human tragedy of the situation also must be placed in the context of a potential widespread armed confrontation in the western hemisphere; our own Vietnam. The situation in Central America hangs like sword of Damocles over the peace and security of the western hemisphere. It is a matter of the most urgent priority. Hence, the Contadora process which we have all supported seemed almost at one point in recent months to have ceased being a process altogether. There seemed to be so little movement in that regard. Now we have seen in the region itself five Presidents agreeing upon a plan, which is ambiguous in many respects and is perhaps somewhat obscure but basically contains very significant elements which could provide for a major breakthrough. These elements include a ceasefire within 90 days, the agreement from each nation not to supply any rebel group which would try to overthrow any existing Central American Government, no attacks to be launched from other Central American countries, reconciliation and amnesty for rebel forces and a process of democratization, internationally-supervised free elections at the end of each Government's present term of office.
September 10, 1987

How wonderful it would be if each of these constituent elements could be addressed by those countries in the region. The situation could become stable and there would be the long-term peace and security that the region so desperately requires. However, already we see that there has been a certain amount of equivocation on the part of Honduras. Again, people might suspect that that might be because of the U.S. policy in the region. Honduras might feel itself obligated and perhaps economically indebted to the United States and it has already raised some questions with respect to verification procedures, allegedly for fear of establishing that there are indeed bases located strategically within its frontiers.
That merely points to the great flaw in this plan which is that it requires more than the support of the region, it desperately requires that of the United States. The United States has said that it is supportive, but Mr. Shultz has said: "We are committed to working with its signatories," referring to the signatories to the Guatemalan peace plan, "to strengthen it, to deal with issues not covered by the agreement, to help gain broad support for its purposes and provisions, but," he said, "it is simply not in our national interest to leave the Sandinista regime unconstrained by credible resistance forces on the basis of a hope or a premise".
In conclusion, let me say that that glimmer of hope which we saw emerging in August must be fanned by goodwill. It must be supported by this Government and, as I have said, apart from the technical assistance and other specific steps we can take in that regard, I believe we must send a strong message to Washington.
Over the last several years, my criticism of the posture of the Government has been that while its policies and its rhetoric in the House against aid to Contras, urging the United States basically to withdraw that support and to help bring a peaceful resolution to the problems in Nicaragua have been supported by all of us and while we continue to provide foreign aid to the area, I do not think that our voice has been heard. I think there has been a reluctance to speak out and to deliver a message to our good friends in Washington as good neighbours and friends should. We should speak frankly and candidly to the Americans on this issue and we should support those Members of Congress and those areas of American public opinion with which we are very much in agreement.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF SIGNING PROTOCOL TO CONTADORA TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to debate the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett). Although the motion has been largely overtaken by events, it still addresses the very difficult and complex situation in Central America. This is an important issue because Central America is the scene of some of the most tragic internecine warfare in the world today and it also has become the scene of serious East-West conflict. It is also important to Canada because it is taking place in the western
Contadora Treaty
hemisphere, in that part of the third world closest to Canada and in a region with which Canada has growing social, economic and political interests.
My hon. friend, the Member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Hudon), has very ably explained the Government's response to the most recent developments in Central America. The emergence of a new peace plan, the initiative of the countries of Central America themselves, is the most encouraging development in the region for several years. As has already been pointed out, the Canadian Government has not stood idly by. While recognizing that Canada has no direct role to play at this stage of the negotiations, we have gone to some lengths to give the maximum possible support and encouragement to the parties. The process of converting the commitments which have been made into a peace settlement will be a difficult one. Our support is more than just rhetorical: the Government stands ready to provide technical advice, where we have the appropriate expertise to offer, in the control and verification process which follows a cease fire in the region.
I want to remind the House, however, that this is not a new approach by the Government. On the contrary, it is entirely consistent with the policies which this Government has pursued with respect to Central America since it was elected. Indeed, our recent effort in support of the new peace plan is a logical extension of the role Canada has sought to play for some time.
Canadian policy towards Central America is a distinct one, shaped by Canadian criteria. It has been developed in recognition of the geopolitical realities of Central America and of the social and economic factors which are at the root of the current problems.
The Canadian Government opposes third party intervention anywhere in Central America and regrets the intrusion into the region of East-West tensions and the related militarization of the area.
Canada does not approve of the supply of armaments by any country to opposing factions in the region. This position has been expressed on numerous occasions to the Governments of Central America, to the United States Government and to the other governments concerned. The United States' decision to provide additional aid to the Contras runs counter to our position. Canada has constantly emphasized its firm belief that the countries of Central America must be free to seek their own solution to their own problems without interference from any outside source.
We strongly share the view that the growth and development of democracy is an important issue in Central America. Canada welcomes the progress which has been made in several countries in the region, while recognizing that there is still room for improvement, particularly in Nicaragua.
Canada does not wish to see Nicaragua locked into the Soviet bloc or involved in destablizing its neighbours. We

September 10, 1987
Contadora Treaty
encourage Nicaragua to move toward the original goals of the Sandinistra revolution which were recently restated in its new constitution: a commitment to political pluralism, a mixed economy and non-intervention in the internal affairs of other countries.
We believe that improvements must be made in the Nicaraguan civil and human rights record. The continued suspension of many basic civil rights under the State of Emergency is profoundly disturbing. We encourage political pluralism in Nicaragua and we support the ability of legitimate domestic political opposition parties to continue to function. We have deplored the decision to close down the La Prensa newspaper, and the harrassment of opposition groups and of the churches. The recent arrest and sentencing of the head of the Nicaraguan Human Rights Commission and the head of the Nicaraguan Bar Association within days of the signing of the peace accord was a disturbing and potentially counterproductive development. It was not consistent with the spirit of the agreement and only served to emphasize the need for reforms within Nicaragua. We hope that the implementation of the peace plan will result in the lifting of the State of Emergency and the removal of the current restrictions on the press and opposition groups and an end to incidents such as that to which I have referred.
The achievement of social justice ranks with the promotion of peace and economic development as one of the highest priorities for Canadian policy in the region. We welcome the fact that the peace plan includes a commitment to representative and pluralist democratic systems of government in all countries in the region.
Human rights violations in Guatemala and El Salvador continue also to be of great concern to the Canadian Government. Canada has been monitoring the human rights situation in both countries, and we have also pursued investigations of a number of cases of particular interest to Canada. Canada has co-sponsored UN General Assembly resolutions expressing deep concern at the continuing violations of human rights in Guatemala, and has voted in favour of resolutions expressing similar concerns in El Salvador.
Canada maintains normal commercial relations with Nicaragua and provides the usual assistance to Canadian firms seeking to do business there. Canada does not support the U.S.A. embargo on trade with Nicaragua, nor has the Government introduced special programs to increase Canadian trade by exploiting the embargo. Nicaragua has established a trading company in Toronto and it is hoped that this initiative will enhance trade opportunities for both countries.
Some critics of the Government's policy on Central America, including the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), have also raised the question of whether Canada should have an embassy in Nicaragua. At present Canada maintains two embassies in Central America, one in San Jose, Costa Rica, accredited to Costa Rica,
Panama, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua, and one in Guatemala City.
The fact that we do not maintain a resident mission in Nicaragua, or indeed in several other Central American countries, does not reflect a political decision on the part of the Canadian Government. The Canadian Government enjoys an excellent working relationship with the Government of Nicaragua, notwithstanding the absence of a resident Canadian Embassy in Managua itself. Ideally, we should like to have resident diplomatic missions in virtually every capital of the world. Economic constraints rule this out. Especially in the current atmosphere of austerity, as the Governement attempts to reduce the national deficit, it would be unrealistic to consider adding to the number of diplomatic posts. In fact, the Government has recently closed a number of missions abroad.
Nevertheless, as a reflection of Canada's growing concern for stability in Central America, the personnel resources of our Embassy in San Jose have been augmented and program responsibilities rearranged in order to be able to devote more attention to Nicaraguan affairs.
It is our view that, through frequent visits to Nicaragua by our Ambassador and his staff (every two weeks on average), we receive accurate and detailed reporting on Nicaragua's domestic political situation, its economic problems and international outreach. Our Embassy has built a wide network of close contacts including, of course, government leaders and senior officials. In addition, the Department of External Affairs maintains close relations with Nicaraguan diplomatic staff in Ottawa, and we discuss Central American issues with many other governments as well as with private organizations in Canada.
There are approximately 50 Canadians residing in Nicaragua who have registered with the embassy in Costa Rica. In addition, a large number of Canadians visit Nicaragua, most in organized groups. Routine consular services of an immediate nature (passport renewal, replacement of stolen documents, et cetera) are provided the British Embassy in Managua. In case of a major emergency, contingency plans are in place to help Canadians leave the country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me reiterate the Government's satisfaction that negotiations for a peaceful settlement in Central America are underway again. We are under no illusions about the serious obstacles which lie in the way of a just peace but Canada stands ready to do what it can to support the process, as the Government has done since it took office.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the introduction of the subject of peace in Central America by my colleague, the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), and move to ask and answer, if I can, the question of why Central America is important to the peace of
September 10, 1987

Canadians. It seems strange in a way. For myself, I have to admit that five and a half years ago I did not know where Tegucigalpa, capital of Honduras, was. I did not know where Managua, capital of Nicaragua, was. However, over the last few years, with many other Canadians, I have been learning fast about the importance of those small countries in Central America.
I found the Central American people to be very lively. I am not referring just to their colours and their dancing and music. 1 mean the refugees I have met are hardy, they survive, and they are loving. They are human, intensely human. In each country a few million people are standing up against the United States and refusing to submit. The Central American peace plan reflects that. That agreement was made despite the pressure of Reagan's diplomats and military threats and dollar subsidies. The churches are also active in both those countries, helping the common people and moving back and forth between those countries and North America, making us aware of what is going on. This enables us to interact and aid each other.
It is a fact that Central Americans in their conduct inspire many Canadians, but the question still remains. I am forced to reflect that our world is emerging from colonialism. Since World War II, India and most of the colonies of the nations of western Europe and North America achieved formal political independence. Economic independence still lags behind. That, after all, was basic. The interest of the European explorers in the Caribbean islands, Central and South America, Africa, India, Southeast Asia and the islands of the Pacific was not mainly a search for political power. Columbus, Vasco Da Gama, Drake, Pizarro and their successors sought spices, gold, sugar, tea, timber, rubber, and a thousand other riches lying plentifully in those countries. They also sought cheap labour to harvest this wealth. They first enslaved the local people so far as it was possible, and then later resurrected the ancient custom of outright slavery and brought an entire black population from Africa to slave in the Western Hemisphere.
Since World War II, European and North American powers have found it inconvenient to continue ruling or controlling these countries directly. The people in these former colonies are no longer satisfied. Yet the controlling countries found it possible for a few years to continue with unequal economic arrangements, unequal sales arrangements, and when necessary enforcing these arrangements through arming or financing and politically supporting whatever local gang of thugs would sell out the goods and labour of their fellow countrymen cheap.
That whole network of post-world war, post-colonial indirect control of the economies of Central America and other colonies is now falling apart. Cuba signalled 28 years ago that it would no longer support us in the style to which we were accustomed. French Indo-China made itself independent from the Japanese by the end of World War II. It was reconquered by Great Britain and France, defeated French rule in 1954, was reinvaded by the U.S., and defeated them in 1975. Many
Contadora Treaty
other former colonial lands have won their economic, military and political freedom or are bent on winning it. Therefore, we have continuing upheavals; local wars, civil wars, revolutions and refugees.
Refugees coming to Canada used to be mainly from eastern Europe and were received respectfully. Now they come mainly from Central America, Africa, Southeast Asia and places like that. Our Government, following the Governments of the U.S. and other NATO countries, now tries to shut them out. These refugees are in fact messengers of the colonial liberation movements. No wonder they bring hope to many Canadians who feel dominated and exploited by the United States of America. No wonder, equally, they bring fear to those who want to continue the old order at home and abroad.
We are finding that a growing number of Canadians who support peace also generally support refugees. They realize that the refugees, regardless of their own intentions sometimes, but because of the reality of their circumstances and the terror which they had to flee in countries like El Salvador, are a symbol of the rejection of the life and rule of war, military control, and the exploitation of men, women and children by the men of war and big business.
The refugees are here. They will continue to come until Canada and Canadians, along with the United States and countries of western Europe recognize that those countries from which the refugees come must be free or we will have no peace.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF SIGNING PROTOCOL TO CONTADORA TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government believes that the basic cause of tension and political conflict in Central America is the deeply rooted socio-economic disparities present in varying degrees in each of the countries in the region. In the Government's view, the most appropriate contribution that Canada can make to the promotion of regional peace and stability is, on the one hand, the provision of development assistance aimed at helping individuals and communities break out of their cycle of poverty and at promoting economic growth in the region and, on the other hand, through support for a regional peace settlement.
Other speakers today have already spoken about the support that Canada has provided and is providing to efforts to achieve a regional peace settlement. I wish to speak for a few moments about Canadian aid to the people of Central America.
Canadian development assistance to Central America began in 1968 with a loan to El Salvador. Following the 1970 foreign policy review, which recommended a higher Canadian profile in the region, aid activities were initiated in all other countries in the region. After the regional program review in 1975, El Salvador and Honduras became CIDA program countries. In 1979, planning for new bilateral projects in El Salvador was suspended as a consequence of the increasingly violent and unstable situation in that country. In 1981, planning for new

September 10, 1987
Contadora Treaty
bilateral projects in Guatemala was also suspended because of internal disorder in that country.
In 1982, following a comprehensive review of Canada's relations with Central America, the Government decided to expand significantly its development assistance program to the countries of Central America. Specifically, the Government decided to allocate up to $106 million in government-to-government aid to the region over the five-year period from 1982-83 to 1986-87. This represented a tripling of the level of bilateral aid provided to the region over the previous five-year period.
With respect to the countries which would benefit from this assistance, it was decided that Honduras, the poorest country in Central America, would be the largest recipient of assistance, as it had been in the past. Costa Rica and Nicaragua would also receive increased allocations of aid. Bilateral aid would remain suspended in Guatemala and El Salvador pending improvements in the internal conditions in those countries.
Further, all countries in the region would be eligible for assistance through other aid channels-the Mission Administered Fund Program, the Non-Governmental Organizations Program, the Institutional Co-operation Program, the Industrial Co-operation Program, the Humanitarian Assistance Program, and the International Development Research Centre.
In December, 1984, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) announced that government-to-govern-ment aid to El Salvador would be resumed. This decision was taken in light of the humanitarian needs of the hundreds of thousands of displaced persons, the economic underdevelopment of El Salvador, the marked improvement in the human rights situation in that country, and the successful return in that country to democratic institutions.
In the five years from 1982-83 to 1986-87, since the Government decided to increase substantially aid to Central America Canada has provided about $106 million in govern-ment-to-government aid to the people of Central America. In other words, the Government has met its commitment to triple the level of government-to-government aid to the region. However, the volume of aid is only half the story. The quality and effectiveness of the aid provided is just as, if not more, important.
We believe that Canada's government-to-government aid to Central America is responding effectively to the particular developmental needs and problems of the individual countries in the region. In Honduras, Canadian government-to-govern-ment aid is supporting the development and conservation of renewable resources, the creation of rural employment, and the improvement of health care and food supplies in rural areas.
In Costa Rica, Canadian government-to-government aid has been used to provide much needed balance of payments support and to fund an important rural housing program. In
Nicaragua, Canada's government-to-government aid has concentrated on basic human needs, food production and energy. In El Salvador, the focus of the government-to-government aid program is assistance to displaced persons and the most disadvantaged.
In addition to the government-to-government aid, during the past five years Canada has provided substantial assistance to the countries of Central America, more than $45 million through other direct assistance channels. These include the Non-Governmental Organizations Program, the Institutional Co-operation Program, the Business Co-operation Program, the Petro-Canada International Assistance Corporation, and the International Development Research Centre.
Further, during the past five years Canada has provided more than $15 million to multilateral organizations such as the United Nations High Commission for Refugees and the International Committee of the Red Cross for their programs to assist refugees and displaced people in Central America.
I believe that Canada, through its official development assistance programs, is responding generously and effectively to the social and economic needs of the people of Central America. On a regional basis Central America is now one of the highest per capita recipients of Canadian official development assistance. The Government and the people of Canada will continue to respond generously to the social and economic needs of the Central American people.
This debate is lacking in that speakers have not pointed out the United States' concern with Communist involvement in Central America. That cannot be ignored. Many Canadians are concerned about the Communist involvement there. It is not one-sided. There are genuine concerns in the United States and here about the Communist infiltration in Central America. The United States must protect itself in that area. That should be on the record. We must lay upon the table that there are genuine concerns and genuine reasons why the United States has involvement in Central America.

So this is a matter-and I know the Hon. Member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Cote) ought to take an interest in these things, it must be understood that the exploitation of man by man can only lead to the kind of events

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-CONTRACT TO VIDEOTAPE BUSINESS EXCELLENCE AWARDS FUNCTION -REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW TENDERING PROCESS
SUPPLY AND SERVICES-CONTRACT TO VIDEOTAPE BUSINESS EXCELLENCE AWARDS FUNCTION -REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW TENDERING PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to expand on a question 1 asked the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Cote) in the House yesterday concerning the contract in Halifax for the Canadian Awards for Business Excellence to be held in September.
The Minister responded in two ways. First, he said that he had examined the case when he heard about it last week and that all regular procedures were followed.
He rather patronizingly suggested in response to my supplementary question that this is, after all, a national event and a Toronto company was given the contract. That is not the point at all. Let me give a few details about this contract. The complaint came from two Nova Scotia companies and one Prince Edward Island company. On July 2, they were given an invitation to tender for this videotaping of an event to be held
Adjournment Debate
at the Halifax Sheraton Hotel. They had to provide information on their tendering price by July 6, which gave them three days to prepare their bid in order to submit it on the fourth day.
In the course of their determining prices for suppliers they discovered that approximately one month previous a company from Toronto had been in Halifax making inquiries and preparing their own bid for this same contract.
One of the companies involved also discovered from an official from the Department of Supply and Services that the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion who was organizing the event had asked that this particular contractor from Toronto, who eventually got the contract, be asked to tender. This person from DRIE who was making this suggestion was also on the committee to select the contractor.
What we have heard from the Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island companies is that this was obviously prearranged so that the Toronto company would get the contract and that between July 2 and July 6, the Department of Supply and Services went through the motions to have a tendering process.
This is the kind of action that is totally contrary to any notion of the Government trying to be fair in contracting to all contractors in the first instance, but certainly contrary to a government whose former Minister of Supply and Services said that his Department will be going out of its way to ensure that companies in the regions which are in need of assistance from the Government for regional disparity purposes are provided with opportunities to take advantage of federal government spending. If all regular procedures had been followed in this case, then obviously those procedures are inadequate. The question put to the Minister yesterday was quite simply this. What procedures are going to be put in place to ensure that there is fairness for Atlantic Canadian companies?
It is quite clear that if the Government wishes to give preference to local companies in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, or wherever these events take place, then it can do so. In this case all these companies were seeking was fairness, for the same opportunity to put in a competitive bid for a contract for work that was to take place in Halifax.
It is not good enough for the Minister to say to the House that, after all, this is a national event. The implication must be that if it is a national event then a Nova Scotia, a Prince Edward Island or a Newfoundland company cannot do it. That is utter nonsense. If that is the attitude of the Government, then we will not see any regional development take place, certainly not through government spending of this type.
I would like to have a more full explanation from the Parliamentary Secretary who I understand will be replying to my question. I would like to see a more full explanation as to

September 10, 1987
Adjournment Debate
what happened in this case, as well as a better explanation as to what procedures are in place and what procedures will be put in place to rectify this situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-CONTRACT TO VIDEOTAPE BUSINESS EXCELLENCE AWARDS FUNCTION -REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW TENDERING PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canada Awards for Business Excellence is an annual national celebration of excellence in Canadian business and is a program of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. Each year a national awards ceremony is held and the winning companies are featured in an audio-visual presentation.
The Department of Supply and Services assists in the selection of the audio-visual production company through requesting and evaluating proposals from industry. This year proposals were requested from five companies-one in Ontario, one in Quebec, and three companies from Atlantic Canada. This is a good cross-section of the industry. Given that the event is national in scope and as three Atlantic production companies were included, this part of the country was more than fairly represented. Indeed, it has been the practice of the Department of Supply and Services through the Atlantic Opportunities Program to extend greater opportunities to companies in Atlantic Canada for participation in national business opportunities.
In the film and video production field alone the Department of Supply and Services increased its contract business volume to Atlantic Canada by 143 per cent during the 1986-87 fiscal year. I can assure the Hon. Member that the Atlantic Opportunities Program launched in April, 1986, is high on the Government's list of priorities.
As Hon. Members are aware, this program represents a new and innovative approach to support regional economic development. In the first year of the program the Department has been successful in bringing new economic opportunities to Atlantic Canada. The bottom-line results of our efforts is that we purchase $573 million worth of goods and services from Atlantic businesses. This represents a $167 million increase over our purchases in 1984-85, the program's base year.
The Department of Supply and Services took a threepronged approach to generating new procurement opportunities in Atlantic Canada. We organized trade shows, business conferences and seminars throughout Atlantic Canada to ensure that businesses were aware of all business opportunities associated with federal procurement needs. I think the Hon. Member will agree that the $167 million increase in all purchasing in Atlantic Canada is something about which we can be proud.
Our efforts to use new policies to bring more contracting opportunities to Atlantic Canadian firms resulted in the following contracts: Ven Rez Products Ltd., Shelbourne, Nova Scotia, $199,947 for modular furniture; Wajax Industries Ltd., Saint John, New Brunswick, $192,360 for a hydraulic crane; Domtar Packaging Inc., Moncton, New Brunswick, $38,428
for shipping boxes; GEC Diesel Inc., St. John's, Newfoundland, $37,500 for a diesel generator.
Our supplier development efforts have helped Novation Information Corp. of Halifax to develop a business information service, and BPL Manufacturing of Spring Hill, Nova Scotia, to develop a new ammunition capability for the Armed Forces.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SPECIAL CANADIAN GRAINS PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION
AGRICULTURE-SPECIAL CANADIAN GRAINS PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 18 last I asked the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) a question on the Special Canadian Grains Program. The Minister replied that this program was being administered in accordance with the rules, guidelines, and criteria that had been established by the Government in close co-operation with 35 or 40 farm leaders.
Today I wish to deal with the administration of this program. First, I wish to stress the fact that this program helped to partially correct the intolerable situation that was created by the subsidy war between the EEC and the U.S. Farm Bill and that this program is helping hundreds of our farmers to stay on the land. At the same time, the program has hurt other farmers. I wish to deal with some of these items now in the hope that correction will be made in any future pay-out, and hopefully in the last one.
During the first pay-out some hay farmers were hurt, and it is questionable as to whether they will be able to stay on the land. Administrators of the program refused to make payments to hay producers. At the same time, the program did recognize farmers who cut their grain crops early and sold it as green feed at lower prices because of the subsidy to feed lots, the major purchasers of hay, thus denying the hay producers their market.
Although the feed lots preferred hay, they could not resist the opportunity to buy feed at a lower price. By the same token, the hay producers could not match the subsidized prices which were below the cost of producing the hay. Consequently, the program helped farmers who produced green feed instead of letting the crops mature and selling the grain, or because weather or other factors prevented the proper maturing of the grain. Properly, the barley producers were helped, but the hay producers had to survive on prices that did not even pay for the production of the hay.
In my constituency, some hay farmers in an attempt to survive tried to sell hay to Japan. They were advised that compressed hay was being subsidized by the Americans. Consequently, again the hay producers could not meet the prices that were being subsidized with public money.
The Hon. Minister advised that he had checked with his farm leaders who were convinced that compressed hay was not being so subsidized. I am presently expecting a letter from the U.S. administrators as to whether it is. If it is not, someone in the United States led our hay farmers down the garden path.
September 10, 1987

In making payment to farmers, the same average yield was used for crops grown on summer fallowed land as was grown on stubble or on irrigated land. Yields on all three are different. While the average for crops grown on stubble and on summer fallow might be reasonably close, they could also be quite different. But yields on irrigated lands may be three or four times higher than those grown on summer fallow or stubble. After the first pay-out, this was brought to the attention of the Minister. This spring in the second pay-out, the error in the payment for irrigated lands was partially corrected. 1 commend the Minister and his administrators for listening to what the farmers had to say, and for making the necessary adjustments.
Elowever, in paying farmers who irrigate on their actual average yield, the administrators decided to limit the payment to farmers who received the water from an irrigation district, while all private irrigators were excluded. This resulted in some 200 or 300 farmers in my riding in southern Alberta being denied the subsidy. These farmers are termed "private" irrigators because they do not belong to an irrigation district, even though they grow the same crops, have equal yields, use the same type of equipment, and have similar costs as those in an irrigation district and have been denied the subsidy.
One difference between farmers who irrigate from a river and those who belong to a district is that a water distribution system of canals and ditches is not necessary. Canals and ditches in irrigation districts are highly subsidized by Governments, whereas the farmers who are being denied any subsidy pay for their machinery and needed equipment.
In my view if land is irrigated and other factors are equal or similar, then payment should also be made to those who are irrigating "privately", as the administrators call it. The so-called "private" farmers in my constituency-and I suppose it is the same elsewhere in Canada-pay a fee to the provincial Government annually for the specific amount of water taken from a river. I have heard that farmers could be dishonest and say that they used more water than they actually did. This would not be possible where the provincial Government or some other municipal district is paid for the water rights and for the amount of water taken out of the river.
Another excuse for no payment to water users is that private irrigators had accepted payment under the drought program in 1985. This is strange, as some farmers who belong to an irrigation district were also paid drought money and properly so. This is unfair treatment of farmers who, through an association or privately, irrigate their land. I am sure every reasonable Canadian will view it as such.
Another unfair item in both payments that was not corrected in the second payment was the yield on summer fallow being the same as that on stubble. There is a difference in production yields.
Adjournment Debate
In addition, the Province of Alberta, by using this method, is taking the chance that some farmers may be paid twice for the same grain-once from the Special Canadian Grains Program and once from the Feed Freight Assistance Program which is operated in Alberta and maybe in other provinces. This is an excuse rather than a reason.
Paying on the seeded acreage encourages farmers to seed to the hilt which in turn this leads to "mining" the soil, which is certainly not in the best interests of the country. Payment on the total acreage is the recommendation of many experienced farmers, and this would not add to the surplus.
Other farmers, including mustard producers and other pulse farmers, now claim that their income was adversely affected because of the depressed climate in agriculture and are very angry at being left out.
In conclusion, 1 urge the Ministers involved in this program to heed the material in this debate, as the points mentioned are not only the views of a Member of Parliament but of a large body of practical farmers who are Canadians too.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pat Binns (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SPECIAL CANADIAN GRAINS PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR INCLUSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has certainly raised some important points in his remarks in relation to the inclusion of hay in this program. I appreciate some of the arguments he has made, especially situations where grain crops were cut as green feed, which of course in turn displaced the hay crop in feed lots and in other areas.
Let me point out again that the $1 billion Special Canadian Grains Program is an interim assistance measure to cushion the impact of the current trade dispute between the European Economic Community and the United States of America. Grain and oilseed prices have been depressed severely because of that subsidy war. Grain and oilseed prices on world markets have been driven down very substantially because of unfair subsidies.
Of course the Government responded by implementing the $1 billion Special Canadian Grains Program. As of September 8, $966 million of that $1 billion program had been mailed out to 200,609 producers. Nearly all the $1 billion has been taken up at this point.
The Special Canadian Grains Program was developed through broad consultation with farm organizations across Canada. It was a consensus of those groups that program benefits should be paid to producers who have been directly and seriously affected by the international subsidy practices, particularly between the EEC and the United States.
Hay was considered when the list of eligible commodities was established. However, the lower prices received for hay last year were felt to be largely the result of normal supply and demand forces.
Canadian hay producers enjoyed an unusually good harvest and today there is still an abundance of hay on domestic

September 10, 1987
Adjournment Debate
markets. Hay prices have not been depressed by international subsidy practices. For this reason, hay was not included in the list of eligible commodities for the Special Canadian Grains Program. Clearly, the aim of this program is not to reward grains and oilseeds producers or to penalize hay producers. The program simply is providing much needed assistance to individuals most seriously affected by the depressed prices on world markets.
As a result of surplus hay production in Canada, the federal Government is currently providing assistance to develop export markets for hay products. One major initiative in this area has been the provision of transportation assistance through the inclusion of pellets and cubes and eligible commodities under the Western Grain Transportation Act. The Government continues to support the efforts of hay producers to maintain and expand markets abroad, and I am pleased to note that despite fierce competition in 1986, the industry successfully maintained its share of foreign markets.
In closing, the Special Canadian Grains Program was an interim measure to deal immediately with lower returns for
1986 crops. One billion dollars was put in place to meet that special need. Our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) along with the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) since that time and in recent weeks and months have been meeting with farm leaders to discuss possible assistance covering the 1987 crop and beyond. It is quite obvious that our Government is committed to helping our farmers. In fact, our assistance has been second to no other government in the past. I know that our Ministers will continue to assist Canadian farmers.
Several options are being considered for the future, and I am sure the remarks of the Hon. Member for Bow River will be given serious consideration by the Ministers in future deliberations.
